en.text: This position comes from a game between Richard Réti and Savielly Tartakower, played in Vienna in 1910. It lasted eleven moves and is still taught as an example of what it costs to leave the king in the centre. It began with a Caro-Kann Defence, where Black answers White’s king pawn advance by moving the queen’s bishop pawn one square. Black brought the queen out early and has just taken a knight on

en.text: Paul Morphy played this game in Paris in 1858, in a box at the opera while a performance was on stage. His opponents were two amateurs, Duke Karl II of Brunswick and Count Isouard, who chose Black’s moves together. It began with the Philidor Defence, named after the same Philidor as the rook ending. Today it is used to teach

en.text: In Spanish it is called the kick mate, because the knight delivers it like a horse’s kick against a king hemmed in by its own pieces. It is a very old pattern: it already appears in Luis Ramírez de Lucena’s book of 1497. In English, the version with a

To defend, give your king a way out in time: one pawn moved in front of the castled king is often enough to stop the knight from finishing.

En aquel juego la torre y el caballo se movían igual que hoy, así que este mate, que solo usa esas dos piezas, ha llegado sin cambios hasta nosotros. El patrón es sencillo. La torre da

en.text: It is one of the oldest known mates: it already appears in medieval Arabic manuscripts, from the days of shatranj, the ancestor of chess. In that game the rook and the knight moved just as they do today, so this mate, which uses only those two pieces, has come down to us unchanged. The pattern is simple. The rook gives

right next to the king, on the edge of the board, and the knight protects it and also covers the square the king could flee to. The king has to be in a corner or very close to one, with no way out. Here Black is ahead in material, but that is worthless if the next move is
. What to remember: before you count pieces, check that your king is safe, and a knight near your corner always deserves a look.
